chunks: And as for what Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
Regarding a man who performed Zihar with his wife four times in one sitting, he said: 'Upon him is one expiation.'

Therefore, this report is to be understood in light of what we previously stated, that the meaning is that he is obligated one expiation in general, rather than one expiation for each of the many times. And it has been narrated that whoever cannot afford emancipation, or feeding sixty poor people, or fasting two consecutive months, should fast eighteen days. This was narrated.

key_terms.إِطْعَامٌ: Feeding (specifically feeding the poor as expiation)
key_terms.ظَاهَرَ: Zihar (a form of divorce where a man declares his wife like his mother's back)
key_terms.كَفَّارَةٌ: Expiation (atonement for a sin or ritual breach)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on Zihar performed multiple times in one sitting?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this report from Imam al-Sadiq by interpreting the 'single expiation' not as a dismissal of multiple acts, but as a unified obligation in kind, reflecting the Shia principle of consolidating repeated minor infractions. The text further highlights the jurisprudential flexibility in expiation methods, noting the specific alternative of eighteen days of fasting for those unable to perform the primary duties, a nuance often discussed in Usuli debates regarding the hierarchy of expiation options.
